spoken: Cross a pea plant that has round seeds with one that has wrinkled seeds, and every seed you get is round.
So the wrinkles just disappear?
That's how it looks. But grow those round seeds into plants, and wrinkled seeds come back, about one in four.
A friar counted thousands of them in a monastery garden, and out of his counts came the first rules of genetics.
This is the story of Gregor Mendel's peas, and of numbers that some called too good to be true.
Mendel was a friar at Saint Thomas's Abbey in Brno, which was called Brünn back then, in the Austrian Empire.
From eighteen fifty-six to eighteen sixty-three, he used the abbey's garden to cross pea plants and follow their offspring.
Why peas, of all plants?
Pea flowers fertilise themselves in the bud, so to cross two plants, Mendel opened a young bud and pulled out its stamens.
And then he dusted it with pollen from another plant.
He called that somewhat laborious, but almost always successful.
He tested 34 varieties, kept 22 that bred true, and picked seven traits, each with two clear forms.
Seeds were round or wrinkled, and yellow or green. Seed coats were grey or white, with violet or white flowers.
Pods were inflated or pinched, green or yellow. Flowers grew along the stem or at the tip, and stems were tall or short.
He chose them that way on purpose. Traits that came in degrees, more or less, he left out.
And he counted. Over those years, he grew and tested some 28,000 plants, most of them peas.
Take seed shape. Mendel crossed plants with round seeds and plants with wrinkled ones.
The shape shows in the seed itself, so he saw the answer that same year. Every seed was round.
He coined the words for it. Round was dominant, and wrinkled, which had vanished, was recessive.
The next year, he sowed those hybrid seeds and let the plants fertilise themselves.
And in their pods, wrinkled seeds were back, often right next to round ones, with nothing in between.
So the wrinkle skipped a generation. Where was it hiding?
First, he counted. From two hundred and fifty-three hybrid plants, he got seven thousand, three hundred and twenty-four seeds.
And 5,474 of them were round, and 1,850 wrinkled.
That's two point nine six round seeds for every wrinkled one, which is close to three to one.
He did the same for all seven traits, and each one landed near three to one, from 2.82 to 3.15.
Seven different traits, and the same ratio every time?
Near enough. All seven together gave 14,949 dominant to 5,010 recessive, which is 2.98 to one.
So why three to one? And how can a trait vanish for a generation, then come back unchanged?
Mendel's answer, in today's words, is that each plant carries two copies of a gene for seed shape, one from each parent.
Let's write the round version as a capital R, and the wrinkled one as a small r.
A hybrid gets a capital R from one parent and a small r from the other, and one capital R is enough to make the seed round.
And the small r? Is it gone?
Not at all. That's dominance. The small r stays hidden, and it can still be passed on.
Each pollen grain and egg cell gets just one copy, so a hybrid's are half capital R and half small r.
And which pollen meets which egg is, in Mendel's own words, a matter of chance.
Like tossing two coins, one for the pollen and one for the egg.
Mendel wrote out the four equally likely meetings as fractions, the pollen over the egg cell.
And only small r over small r, one in four, makes a wrinkled seed.
The other three hold a capital R, so they're round.
Today the same bookkeeping is drawn as a square, which Reginald Punnett devised decades later.
It predicts one pure round, two hybrids and one pure wrinkled, in every four.
Which means two round seeds in three should be hybrids, still hiding a small r. And Mendel tested that.
How do you test for something you can't see?
You grow the seed, and look at the seeds its plant makes.
Of 565 plants grown from round seeds, 372 made both kinds of seed, and 193 made only round ones.
That's one point nine three to one, close to the two to one he predicted.
Next, Mendel crossed plants that differed in two traits, round yellow seeds with wrinkled green ones.
The hybrids were all round and yellow. From fifteen of them, he harvested five hundred and fifty-six seeds, in four kinds.
There were 315 round yellow seeds, 101 wrinkled yellow, 108 round green, and 32 wrinkled green.
And two of those kinds are new. Round green and wrinkled yellow don't look like either original parent.
If the two traits are inherited separately, three quarters of the seeds are round, and three quarters of those are yellow.
That makes nine sixteenths round and yellow, and the four kinds come in nine, three, three and one.
For 556 seeds, that predicts about 313 round yellow and 35 wrinkled green, with 104 of each mixed kind.
And he got three hundred and fifteen, and thirty-two. That's close.
So seed shape and seed colour had sorted independently.
With three traits, he found twenty-seven kinds, and he bred all one hundred and twenty-eight pure combinations of the seven.
Mendel presented all of this to the Natural History Society of Brno, at two meetings in February and March 1865.
About forty people listened, and his paper came out in the society's journal in eighteen sixty-six.
And then, the famous silence?
Not total silence. But it was read as a paper on hybrids, and cited only about three times in thirty-five years.
Even Mendel seems to have thought his rules held only for some kinds of plants.
His hawkweed crosses didn't fit, since many hawkweeds, it turned out, make most of their seeds without fertilisation.
Then he became abbot, and his duties largely ended his science. He died in 1884.
In the spring of nineteen hundred, three plant scientists in three countries published within about two months, all pointing back to Mendel.
They were Hugo de Vries in the Netherlands, Carl Correns in Germany, and Erich von Chermak in Austria.
Three at once, after thirty-four years. Was that a coincidence?
Not entirely. Botanists were already hunting for a theory of inheritance without blending.
Historians now doubt that Chermak understood Mendel's laws, and how much de Vries owed to Mendel is still debated.
And in England, William Bateson championed the work so hard he was called Mendel's bulldog. He named the new science genetics.
Three to one is an average, though. Plant by plant, Mendel's counts wandered.
His first ten plants for seed shape gave 45 to 12, then 27 to 8, then 24 to 7.
One gave nineteen to ten, under two to one. And another, he noted, gave forty-three to two.
If that were your only plant, you'd never guess three to one.
Small counts swing widely, because chance decides which pollen meets which egg.
So let's have chance do the same. For every seed, we pick capital R or small r for the pollen, and again for the egg.
Here are ten imaginary plants, with the same numbers of seeds as Mendel's first ten.
And they scatter just like his, from twenty-one to eleven on one plant, to twenty-nine to five on another.
Now let's keep going, seed after seed.
After 40 seeds, the ratio stands at 7 to one. After 400, it has fallen to 3.30 to one.
And by seven thousand, three hundred and twenty-four seeds, as many as Mendel counted, it has settled at three point one to one.
Mendel put it this way. The larger their number is, the more mere chance effects are eliminated.
In 1936, the statistician Ronald Fisher tested how well Mendel's numbers fit.
Real counts miss a prediction by chance. Mendel's, Fisher argued, missed by too little.
Too little? How can data be too good?
Chance always leaves some scatter. Counts that hug the prediction every time are strange in their own way.
Against 1,000 gardens run by chance alone, only 50 come as close to three to one as Mendel's seven totals.
That's about one garden in twenty. Lucky, but not shocking.
Fisher's point was that the luck kept repeating.
His sharpest point was a test in which Mendel grew ten offspring of each plant.
That was to tell the pure plants from the hybrids, right?
Yes, but a hybrid's ten can all look dominant by chance, so he should have found about one point seven, not two.
And he reported 399 hybrids to 201 pure, almost exactly two to one.
Fisher concluded that most of the data had been falsified, perhaps by an assistant who knew too well what was expected.
That's a heavy charge, made more than fifty years after Mendel died.
Daniel Hartl and Daniel Fairbanks replied that Mendel probably grew more than ten, and that the fraud charge could be put to rest.
Their 2008 book with others, called Ending the Mendel Fisher Controversy, found no reason to think he made up results.
Yet one of its own authors, A W F Edwards, still found too little scatter in 84 of Mendel's ratios.
One can applaud the lucky gambler, he wrote, but when he is lucky again tomorrow, and the next day, and the following day,
one is entitled to become a little suspicious.
So the book meant to end the controversy didn't quite end it.
Then a twenty nineteen reanalysis, adding the extreme plants Mendel himself reported, found about as much scatter as chance predicts.
And Mendel also said he left out some small experiments that strayed.
So the open question is how he chose, counted and reported his peas, not whether he grew them.
Mendel never knew what his factors were made of. For the wrinkled seed, the answer came in nineteen ninety.
Wrinkled seeds lack one form of an enzyme that builds starch, called starch-branching enzyme one.
In wrinkled peas, its gene is interrupted by an extra stretch of DNA, about eight hundred letters long.
And the intruder looks like a jumping gene known from maize.
Without the enzyme, the young seed makes less starch and keeps more sugar, which draws in extra water.
So a wrinkled seed starts out swollen?
Yes, and then, as the ripe seed dries out, it ends up wrinkled.
One working copy of the gene makes the enzyme, so the seed stays round. That's dominance, in chemistry.
So dominant just means one good copy is enough.
It was the first of Mendel's seven genes to be found, and by twenty twenty-five, all seven had been identified.
So here is what the peas were saying. Every plant carries two copies of each gene, one from each parent.
Each pollen grain and each egg cell gets one of them, by chance.
A recessive copy can hide for a generation, and shows again when two hidden copies meet, one time in four.
None of this shows in a single pod. It appears only when someone counts thousands.
Which is why the counting mattered as much as the crossing.
His counts waited 34 years to be understood, and then they became the first rules of genetics.
All from a friar, a garden, and a careful count of peas.
